sections.label: Organization Overview and Eligibility
sections.text:
Black Mamas Village (EIN 88-1025060; blackmamasvillage-atx.org)[^1] is a Black-led peer-support and mutual-aid organization serving Black mothers across greater Austin, under the tagline "Where Every Black Mother Belongs"[^2]. It began as a Facebook group in June 2019, was recognized by the IRS as a 501(c)(3) in September 2023[^1], and now operates The Village Place, a 6,500-square-foot community hub at 8401 North IH-35 in Austin with childcare space, co-working space, a library, and a dedicated nap room for mothers[^3]. Its work runs on three pillars: Connection and Belonging, Economic Empowerment, and Health and Wellness[^2].

Against the fund's three pass/fail eligibility gates[^4][^5], this application clears all three. Registered 501(c)(3): met, recognized September 2023[^1]. Serves the Greater Austin area: met, with a physical hub in Travis County and a service area across greater Austin[^2][^3]. BIPOC-led, which requires meeting at least two of three tests: the mission-and-programs test is met on the organization's face, since it exists specifically to serve Black mothers[^2], and the senior-leadership test is met by its Black-led, co-directive leadership[^2].

[CONFIRM: the current share of the board of directors who identify as BIPOC. The organization very likely satisfies all three tests rather than the two required, but the board figure was not found in public sourcing, and a claim this easy to state precisely should be stated precisely rather than implied.]

sections.label: Organizational Need and Readiness
sections.text:
This is scored criterion 1: how clearly the organization demonstrates a fundraising challenge, and its readiness to implement the project[^5].

The challenge is visible in the organization's own filings. Revenue grew from $84,481 in FY2023, its first filed year, to $301,071 in FY2024, to $560,326 in FY2025, roughly a 6.6x increase in two years, and is reported as nearly 100% contributions in each of those years[^1]. That growth is real, and it is also the problem: it arrived through a small number of large institutional awards rather than through a broad base of donors. A single grant, the $80,000 unrestricted Impact Austin award in 2025[^6], accounts for roughly 14% of FY2025 revenue by itself. An organization whose income is almost entirely contributed, and whose largest contributions are concentrated in a handful of grantmakers with their own cycles and cooldowns, is one denied application away from a hard year. That fragility is precisely what this fund exists to address.

[MISSING: an inventory of the organization's current fundraising infrastructure. Specifically: whether it uses a donor database or CRM and which one; whether any staff member or co-lead holds development as a named responsibility; whether a recurring-giving program exists; whether a written annual fund plan exists; and how many individual donors gave in FY2025, at what average gift. This is the most load-bearing missing item in the entire application. Scored criteria 1, 2, and 6 all depend on it, none of it is public, and only the organization can supply it. A reviewer scoring a 4 here needs to see the gap named concretely, with numbers, not gestured at.]

[CONFIRM: which two people will own this project, and roughly how many hours a week each can give it. The rubric looks explicitly for leadership commitment and implementation capacity, not need alone[^5]. The organization's horizontal, co-directive model, "each one, reach one, and teach one"[^2], is an asset here and should be named as one: this project would be carried by a pair of co-leads rather than resting on a single executive's calendar.]

sections.label: Fundraising Capacity-Building Impact
sections.text:
This is scored criterion 2, the extent to which the project strengthens long-term fundraising effectiveness[^5]. It is the heart of the application.

[SUGGESTED project: build Black Mamas Village's first individual-giving program, consisting of a donor CRM, a written annual fund plan, and AFP training for two co-leads.] The reasoning comes from the organization's own numbers rather than from a template. Revenue is almost entirely contributed and concentrated in institutional awards[^1][^6], which means the missing leg is a broad, repeatable base of individual donors. And the organization already holds the ingredient that is hardest to manufacture: a community of more than 3,000 Black mothers who already know it and already trust it[^2] (a self-reported figure; see the gaps list). What it does not yet demonstrably have is the machinery to turn that community into recurring revenue.

This proposal maps onto three of the six project types AFP itself names as eligible: annual fund planning, staff training, and fundraising technology[^4]. It also puts the non-cash half of the award to work rather than treating it as a bonus. The two AFP memberships and two One Day Conference tickets fit the organization's co-lead structure exactly: two people trained together, which is how this organization actually operates, rather than one executive sent to learn alone.

The long-term effect, and the thing to say plainly to a reviewer, is that the project converts one-time community goodwill into revenue that renews on its own and belongs to no single funder's cycle. That is a permanent change in fundraising capacity, not a one-year bump.

[MISSING: the organization's own decision about what to build. The project above is this draft's proposal, not the organization's choice, and a reviewer is scoring the organization's conviction, not a consultant's. If the real priority is a development audit, a feasibility study for a capital campaign at The Village Place, or grant-writing capacity instead, the case is just as makeable, but the application has to be rebuilt around it. Decide this first: everything downstream depends on it.]

sections.label: Project Feasibility (9-Month Plan)
sections.text:
Criterion 3 asks whether the project is realistic, well planned, and achievable inside the 9-month grant period[^5]. Awards are announced August 31, 2026[^4], so the working window runs from roughly September 2026 through May 2027.

One piece of timing is worth naming for the reviewer, because it shows the plan was built against the real calendar: the AFP Greater Austin One Day Conference falls on October 9, 2026[^4], which lands inside month 2 of the grant period. The two conference tickets are usable while the project is live, feeding directly into the work, rather than arriving as a perk after it ends.

[SUGGESTED 9-month timeline:]

Months 1 to 2 (September to October 2026): development audit and contact-data cleanup. Select and configure the CRM, and migrate existing contact lists into it.

Months 2 to 3 (October to November 2026): the two co-leads activate their AFP memberships and attend the One Day Conference on October 9, 2026.

Months 3 to 5 (November 2026 to January 2027): write the annual fund plan. Segment the list, and design the donor journey from first touch to recurring gift.

Months 5 to 7 (January to March 2027): run the first live test, a year-end and new-year giving campaign, against the new list and the new plan.

Months 7 to 9 (March to May 2027): measure results, set a recurring-giving baseline, document what worked, and report to AFP.

[CONFIRM: that this sequence is achievable alongside the organization's existing program commitments, and who is accountable for each phase. A timeline a reviewer believes is one whose owner the organization can name.]

sections.label: Use of Funds (Budget Narrative)
sections.text:
Criterion 4 scores whether the requested funds are clearly and strategically tied to project activities and to fundraising capacity building[^5]. The award is a fixed $10,000 in cash plus the two memberships and two conference tickets[^4], so there is no amount to negotiate. What is being scored is whether the $10,000 is aimed at capacity, or quietly at program delivery, which this fund does not support[^4].

[SUGGESTED: $3,000, donor CRM. Selection, configuration, migration of existing contacts, and the first-year subscription.] [MISSING: actual vendor quotes. Get two.]

[SUGGESTED: $4,500, fundraising consultant. A development audit and a written annual fund plan the organization keeps and reuses. AFP Greater Austin publishes a consultant referral list for exactly this purpose[^4], and drawing the consultant from AFP's own list is a small, free signal of fit.]

[SUGGESTED: $1,500, campaign production. Design, print, postage, and digital costs for the first year-end giving campaign, which is the project's live test rather than a marketing expense.]

[SUGGESTED: $1,000, staff time. A stipend recognizing the two co-leads who carry this project on top of existing duties. Naming this is more honest than pretending the labor is free, and it answers the rubric's implementation-capacity question directly.]

[SUGGESTED: total, $10,000, matching the award exactly.]

sections.label: Inclusion, Diversity, Equity, and Access (IDEA)
sections.text:
This is scored criterion 5, and it is where applications with a genuinely strong case still lose points. The rubric awards a 4 only where there are "specific examples and evidence of implementation"; a statement of commitment without examples scores a 2[^5]. Read the criterion closely: it asks how IDEA is incorporated into the organization's fundraising practices as well as its overall work[^5]. The fundraising half is the half applicants skip.

The structural case is strong on its face and should be made first, briefly. Black Mamas Village is a Black-led organization serving Black mothers in a city where Black residents are roughly 6% of a fast-growing population[^2], and it is governed horizontally, with each program pillar run by a pair of co-leads rather than a single director[^2]. Its leadership composition is not an aspiration it is working toward. It is the organization.

[MISSING: two or three specific, dated examples of IDEA inside fundraising practice itself, which is what separates a 3 from a 4 here. Candidates the organization may already be doing without counting them as fundraising: community input into how unrestricted dollars get spent; free or sliding-scale access to events that also function as donor events; fundraising materials written in the community's own voice rather than in a deficit frame; childcare, transportation, and accessibility accommodations at events; donor recognition that does not rank people by gift size. Use the ones that are true, with dates and specifics. Do not claim the ones that are not.]

sections.label: Organizational Budget
sections.text:
This is scored criterion 6, and it is the one place this application gives up points. It is worth being precise about that rather than anxious about it.

AFP gives preference to organizations with annual operating budgets of $500,000 or less[^4]. Two things become clear on reading the rubric itself. First, this is a scored criterion, one of six worth 4 points each on a 24-point scale, and it is not an eligibility gate: the only pass/fail gates are 501(c)(3) status, Greater Austin service area, and BIPOC-led status[^5]. Being over the line disqualifies no one. Second, the rubric explicitly contemplates organizations above the threshold and tells reviewers how to score them: an organization over $500,000 that "demonstrates limited fundraising infrastructure and significant need for capacity-building support" scores 3 of 4, while one with "substantial fundraising infrastructure and access to fundraising resources" scores 1[^5].

Black Mamas Village's FY2025 figures are a total revenue of $560,326 and total expenses of $346,762[^1].

[CONFIRM: which figure the organization's board-approved annual operating budget actually uses, and report here the same number the organization reports elsewhere. Funders commonly read "operating budget" as the expense budget, which would place Black Mamas Village under the $500,000 line and score a 4. But this must be the organization's real, consistently reported figure. Do not pick the more favorable number after the fact: a budget that contradicts the organization's own Form 990 or its other applications costs far more credibility than the single point it would save.]

Even on the least favorable reading, the arithmetic is reassuring rather than alarming. Sections 2 and 3 of this application make exactly the case the rubric rewards with a 3: limited fundraising infrastructure, significant need for capacity-building support. The worst case therefore forfeits one point out of twenty-four, leaving a ceiling of 23, which sits inside AFP's own Highly Competitive band of 22 to 24[^5]. This is a fundable application, not a compromised one.

None of this is public. Scored criteria 1, 2, and 6 all depend on it, which makes it the most important gap in the application.

factors.assessment: Strong. Clears all three pass/fail gates cleanly: a 501(c)(3) since September 2023, a Greater Austin service area with a physical hub in Travis County, and BIPOC-led on at least two of the fund's three tests, and probably all three.

Was decisive when this draft was written, and is now the weakest part of it. This was the only researched opportunity with a confirmed open deadline at the time, which is why it became the sample; that deadline of July 31, 2026 has since passed and AFP has posted no next cycle. Re-aim this draft at the next AFP cycle. Separately, and unrelated to AFP, The Black Fund is open and closes September 10, 2026, which is where the near-term drafting effort belongs.
Strong. Five of the six scored criteria are squarely winnable, and the organization's revenue concentration is a textbook fit for a fund built to address exactly that fragility.

A known, bounded cost. FY2025 revenue exceeds the $500,000 preference line, but this is a scored criterion rather than a gate, and the rubric awards 3 of 4 to over-threshold organizations with limited fundraising infrastructure. Worst case is 23 of 24, still Highly Competitive.

The real weakness. The organization's actual fundraising infrastructure, which criteria 1, 2, and 6 all turn on, is entirely non-public. This draft names that gap rather than inventing an answer, but the organization has to fill it before this is submission-ready.

Unknown, and worth saying so. Two organizations are selected, the application is low-lift, and the applicant pool is not published. A strong application is well worth writing; no application here is safe.

strength_analysis.summary: Written when this was the strongest realistic move on the board and the only one that could be filed at the time. That is no longer true of the timing: the 2026 cycle closed on July 31, 2026. Everything the draft says about fit still holds, so read this as a draft ready to re-aim at AFP's next cycle. Eligibility is clean, the fund's purpose matches the organization's actual structural weakness (a 6.6x revenue climb built almost entirely on a handful of institutional grants), and the budget concern that dominated the first research pass turns out to cost at most one point of twenty-four. What stands between this draft and a submission is not funder risk. It is roughly an hour of the organization's own information, most of it about fundraising infrastructure that only the organization can describe.

drafts.funder: The Black Fund of Central Texas (fiscally sponsored by Austin Community Foundation)
drafts.priority_rationale: Now the top of the list, as of August 26, 2026, because the AFP cycle above it closed rather than because anything here improved. The best fit on paper and the strongest relationship: explicitly focused on Black-led organizations rather than narrowly on health, Central-Texas place-based, publishing no minimum-budget or years-of-operation floor, and Black Mamas Village is already a confirmed grantee ($5,000, 2023 inaugural cycle). OPEN NOW AND CLOSING SEPTEMBER 10, 2026.
